title: The fire sermon
hookLine: to a thousand fire-worshipers: all is burning, with greed, hate and delusion (SN 35.28)

lines: UP THE HILL AT GAYA HEAD.
cards: Coaches talk in plays. Musicians talk in songs. The way into a room is often through what it already knows.
The Buddha has walked back to Uruvela, near the tree of his awakening, and meets three brothers named Kassapa: well-known teachers with matted hair, who with their followers number about a thousand.
Their whole religious life is tending sacred fires, keeping the flames going, making offerings into them.
The old texts tell of wonders and long nights before the brothers are won over; then they throw their hair and their fire tools into the river.

teach.b: It begins, in the texts, with one stark sentence: everything, monks, is burning. And what is burning? The eye, what the eye sees, the seeing itself.
The ear, and sounds. The nose, and smells. The tongue, the body, the mind, and everything they touch.
With the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. With birth, aging and death, with sorrow and grief and despair. Hear it as a fire-keeper would.
You've fed flames every day of your life, and now someone points at your own eyes and says: there's the fire. You don't have to climb a hill to find it. It's in the wanting, the anger, the confusion.
Then the turn. Someone who sees this, he says, grows tired of feeding it. They become disenchanted, and cool.
The wanting fades, and with its fading, they are free. The texts say that as they listened, the thousand were freed too.
Some teachers connect that cooling to nibbana, nirvana, a word Pali also uses for a fire going out, the way a lamp goes out when its oil is used up. And it traveled a long way. In 1922, the poet T.

teach.h: A SERMON IN A MODERN POEM.
teach.b: Eliot named a whole section of The Waste Land The Fire Sermon, and ended it with the word burning, over and over.
A talk on a hill in India turned up in a well-known poem in English.

how: The Fire Sermon (Adittapariyaya Sutta) is studied and chanted in Theravada communities, and Buddhist teachers use its three fires, greed, hatred and delusion, to explain what nibbana puts out.

o: the fires of hell that punish wrongdoers
a sacred fire kept alight for offerings
burning, as with greed, hate and delusion

games.q: what's inside the sermon — tap the pairs.
p: a 1922 poem with a Fire Sermon

s: the fire sermon was taught to people who worshiped fire
about a thousand followers of the three Kassapa brothers.
the sermon says the world outside is on fire, so run from it
the fire is in the senses and the mind: greed, hatred, delusion.
some teachers link nibbana to a flame going out
Pali uses the word for a fire going out, like a lamp when its oil is gone.

games.q: you're teaching a thousand people who have spent their lives tending sacred fires. how do you begin?
o: tell them everything, even their own eyes, is burning.
teach them a new ritual with water.
games.why: he speaks their language: everything is burning, the eye, the ear, the mind, with greed, hatred and delusion. and seeing it cools it.

practice: Scan yourself slowly, like checking a house for heat: wanting that pulls toward a screen, a snack, a person; irritation, a hot spot about something someone said; fog, a place you'd rather not look.
Don't fight any of it; just find the warm places and name them, wanting, anger, fog. Then breathe out slowly, as if you were cooling soup.

wordCard.voice: Aditta. Burning: taught to a thousand fire-keepers on Gaya Head, the senses burn with greed, hatred and delusion, and seeing it lets them cool.

orig.note: Pali: burning, set on fire. The sermon is the Adittapariyaya, the discourse on burning.

carryVoice: Your line: all is burning. Seeing the fire is where the cooling starts. Rest well.

sources.ref: T. S. Eliot, The Waste Land, part III (1922)
